title: Who Sells What to Whom: Business Models and the Economics That Shape Architecture
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/02-commerce-business-models/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter. It is a contract, not a description: the places where the chapter does not yet do what the spec asks are listed under open_questions.

know: The commerce business models and what each changes: who captures the order, sets the price, is the legal seller, holds the stock and ships.
The four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), defined by shape.
believe: Systems follow from the business model and its unit economics, not from the technology.
can_do: Place their own company in a business model and a scale stage, and say which numbers pull hardest on its architecture.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the product manager, analyst or consultant who has to turn a business plan into system requirements, and the engineer who has only ever seen one business line. Leaders deciding whether business lines or brands should share a stack get the trade-off and its conditions.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side.
Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
Kestrel & Pine, its people and its 2026 incidents, in outline (meet-kestrel-and-pine), and the names of the failure patterns (where-commerce-platforms-go-wrong).

From journey-of-an-order: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, what a system is, 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, the seven systems at Kestrel & Pine, the names of the four scale stages, and PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and availability service.
does_not_know: The model names: B2C, D2C, wholesale, B2B e-commerce, B2B2C, marketplace selling and operating, omnichannel, subscription.
Seller of record, GMV, EDI-type sales, VAT, punchout, parity rules, repricing, tenancy, POS, OMS, PIM, ASN.
Commerce finance vocabulary: conversion rate, cart abandonment, average order value, gross margin, landed cost, contribution, interchange, chargeback, customer acquisition cost.
Scale stage as a shape; the three arrangements (one stack, a stack per line, a shared core with line-specific edges).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a short description of a merchant, the reader assigns it a scale stage and justifies the choice by channels, locations and brands, not by revenue.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand sells online in two countries, has opened three stores and has just started on one marketplace. Which stage is it in, and what told you?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Omnichannel (or moving from Growing to Omnichannel), argued from channels and stock locations.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given one way of selling, the reader says who captures the order, who sets the price, who is the seller of record, who holds the stock and who ships.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand lists its jacket on someone else's marketplace and sends each order from its own warehouse. Using only this chapter: who captures the order, who sets the price, who is the seller of record, who holds the stock and who ships?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The marketplace captures the order (the seller imports it); the seller sets the price, under the marketplace's parity rules; the seller (the brand) is the seller of record; the seller holds the stock; the seller ships.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two of a merchant's numbers, the reader names the part of the architecture each pulls on.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant finds that 24% of the items it sells online come back and that its busiest hour carries about 41 times the traffic of an average hour. Using only this chapter: which parts of its systems do these two numbers say must be strongest, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The return rate pulls on the reverse flow (restocking, refunding and crediting across systems), which must be designed, not bolted on; the peak pulls on capacity of the whole chain, every integration included, not only the storefront.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a merchant with several lines, the reader says which of the three arrangements the chapter recommends and what is shared and what is kept per line.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant runs its web shop and a small wholesale line on one system. A second system has now started writing prices that the first one also writes. Using only this chapter: what does the author recommend, and what would be shared between the lines and what kept separate?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Move to a shared core with line-specific edges: the facts every line shares (product, price list, stock, order record) are owned once; the promises that differ per line stay at the edges (consumer checkout, B2B portal, till, marketplace listing). Not a stack per line.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader new to commerce meets no term in this chapter before it is explained, and every acronym is expanded on first use.

thesis.question: Why do a D2C brand, a wholesaler, a retailer with stores, a marketplace seller and a marketplace operator need different systems?
thesis.claim: A business model is a decision about who makes which promise, so the systems a merchant needs follow from who captures the order, sets the price, is the legal seller, holds the stock and ships, and its scale stage is defined by that shape rather than by revenue.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that commerce is one problem with one best platform, and that merchants differ only in size.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that copies the architecture of a company with a different model or shape buys problems it does not have and leaves its own unsolved.
thesis.how_why: Each unit-economics number pulls on a different part of the platform (conversion on checkout, returns on the reverse flow, the peak day on capacity), and each added channel or location turns the joins between systems into the problem.

supporting_claims.claim: Lines that sell the same product ask different things of the systems, because each carries a different business obligation.
The business models are distinct in ways that can be defined and counted, and a merchant usually runs several at once.
A business model is a decision about who makes and keeps each promise of an order, and those answers decide what the systems must do.
Each number in the unit economics of an order, the peak included, pulls on a different part of the platform.
A scale stage is a shape of business, set by channels, stock locations, countries and brands, and each transition adds joins between systems.
What the lines share should be owned once and what differs kept at the edges; lines forced together or kept apart without that fail in ways particular to each model.

role.contribution: Explains why the same journey needs different systems for different merchants, and defines the four scale stages every later chapter compares against.

additional_patterns.applies_to: in-practice and when-it-goes-wrong: parallel findings and parallel incidents
when-it-goes-wrong then choices: the incidents, then the arrangement that prevents them

flow.rationale: The scene gives four different requests and so poses the question of what the lines share. The models come next because the requests cannot be compared until the lines have names; the promise table follows the definitions because it needs the model names as its columns. The public record follows the promise table directly: four of its five findings confirm the definitions, and read five sections later they would send the reader back to figures already forgotten; it also establishes marketplace operating as a different business long before the recommendation warns against copying it. The economics follow because a number means nothing until the reader knows whose promise it pays for; the worked example applies promises and numbers to one jacket, and the peak closes the numbers as the one no single order shows; placed before the metrics it would be a load with nothing to weigh it against. The stages come after the models and numbers because a stage is defined by how many models, channels and locations a merchant runs; before them 'three or four models on one stock' would name things the reader has not met. The stages end on the slowed market, which says where merchants now compete, and the incidents follow directly because that is where they sit. The incidents come directly before the choices: they are the problem the three arrangements answer, and told after the choices they would re-derive the remedy the recommendation has already given. The choices come last because they are the chapter's answer and need everything before them: put first, 'a shared core' would be a shape with no reason; put before the incidents, 'the joins cost money' would be asserted and not shown.

hook.content: A brand's web shop sells a jacket to a shopper; its wholesale team sells the same jacket to a retail chain. Software built for the first sale can accept the second order yet fail to meet its conditions.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone can picture the same product sold to a person and to a shop.
bridge.to_topic: The two sales carry different obligations (an agreed price, a delivery date and a return right against a contract price, labeled pallets and a readable invoice), and so do selling on a marketplace and running one: the differences are the business models.

thesis_statement.text: A business model is a decision about who makes which promise; the systems follow from that, not from the technology, and scale stages are defined by shape, not revenue.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout, first and third bullets; paragraph p02 states the premise in prose

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and paragraph p03

promises.promise: Start from what the people running Kestrel & Pine's four lines asked of technology.
Explain the business models, by definition and by who makes which promise, and check both against the public record.
Follow the money an order earns and costs, through one jacket in three lines and through the peak.
Show how the lines failed over facts they shared and nobody owned, and answer what four lines should share and what must stay separate.

evidence.shows: The same product and a similar-looking order carry different conditions, which is the chapter's subject in one case.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Marketplace sellers and marketplace operators carry yet other obligations, so orders that look alike can create very different obligations.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eva's jacket from the previous chapter is a consumer purchase; the same jacket also leaves Kestrel & Pine, the fictional outdoor brand, by a wholesale reorder, a marketplace order or a store sale, and these are the company's four business lines, each needing a different route from order to payment and delivery.

transition_in.carries_over: Orders that look alike and carry different obligations.
transition_in.introduces: The four routes one jacket takes out of the running example's company, its four business lines.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter starts from what the people running the four lines asked of technology, explains the business models by definition and by who makes which promise and checks both against the public record, follows the money an order earns and costs through one jacket in three lines and through the peak, defines the four scale stages, shows how the lines failed over facts they shared and nobody owned, and ends on the practical question of what four business lines should share and what must stay separate.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: One Jacket, Four Ways to Sell It
sections.controlling_idea: Asked what they needed from technology, the people who run Kestrel & Pine's four lines each named a different obligation, so the task is to find what the lines can share and what each must keep.

advances_thesis.how: Shows in one company that lines selling the same product ask different things of the systems.

flow.rationale: The accounts, the question, the answers, then what the answers have in common: the reader hears the requests before being told they are different obligations.

transition_in.carries_over: One jacket leaving the company by four routes.
transition_in.introduces: The company's four lines in figures and what the people running them asked for.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In February 2027 Noor Visser and the finance director reviewed the accounts before proposing Waypoint: €48.0 million of 2026 revenue from four lines that share one warehouse and one catalog.

evidence.what: 2026 revenue €48.0 million at 54% gross margin: €27.0 million online, €12.0 million wholesale, €6.0 million through six stores, €3.0 million through three marketplaces; one warehouse in Duiven, 3,400 products.
evidence.shows: The four lines are real businesses of different size that already share stock and catalog.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Noor then asked the people who run the four lines what they needed from technology in 2027.

transition_in.carries_over: The review of the four lines' accounts.
transition_in.introduces: The question put to the people who run them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The storefront and marketplace manager asked for completed checkouts, credible delivery dates and fresher marketplace stock, while the wholesale lead asked for correct contract prices, fewer hand-typed orders and an end to chargebacks, the deductions a retailer takes from an invoice when a delivery breaks its rules.

evidence.what: 38% of wholesale orders were still typed from email into the ERP.
evidence.shows: The wholesale line's need is of a different kind from the consumer line's.

transition_in.carries_over: The question Noor asked.
transition_in.introduces: The answers of the two people who sell.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Operations asked that pallets and parcels stop competing for the same pickers and that the web shop see store stock, and finance asked for one definition of an order.

evidence.what: Daniel Okafor's and Sanne de Wit's requests.
evidence.shows: Even the functions shared by all lines feel the lines' differences.

transition_in.carries_over: The answers of the two selling leads.
transition_in.introduces: The answers of the two people who serve every line.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each request exposed a different business obligation, so Noor's proposal had to identify the facts the four lines could share and the rules each needed to keep.

transition_in.carries_over: The four sets of requests.
transition_in.introduces: What they have in common, and the task that follows: separate shared facts from line-specific rules.

sections.heading: The Business Models, Defined by the People Who Report Them
sections.controlling_idea: The model names have exact definitions in statistics and annual reports, and a merchant usually runs several models at once.

advances_thesis.how: Gives each model a definition that can be counted, so the later sections can say what each one changes.

transition_in.carries_over: The four lines and their different requests.
transition_in.introduces: The names of the business models those lines are instances of, with exact definitions.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Marketing uses the model names loosely, while statistics agencies and annual reports define them precisely because they have to count something, and their definitions distinguish nine models.

evidence.what: Nine models (B2C, D2C, wholesale, B2B e-commerce, B2B2C, marketplace selling, marketplace operating, omnichannel, subscription), each with a working definition and the report or agency that uses it.
evidence.shows: Each name can be tied to a definition somebody counts by, so the names can be used exactly.
evidence.source: Eurostat (February 2026); VF, Columbia, Zalando, Amazon and Target annual reports (2026)

evidence.what: Figure 1: nine small scenes, one per model.
evidence.shows: Each model is a different answer to who sells, to whom and through whose channel, and a merchant usually runs several.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three terms in the table need plain words: the seller of record is the party that legally sells to the customer, GMV is the value of orders passing through a platform including what it does not keep, and EDI-type sales are orders received as structured messages between systems.

evidence.what: Shopify's 2025 annual report defines GMV as 'the total dollar value of orders facilitated through our platform' net of refunds; Amazon states it is not the seller of record for third-party sales.
evidence.shows: The terms are the companies' own, used where money and liability are reported.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the invoice links shopper and seller, a GMV stack with a small fee kept, EDI at 11.07% against web sales at 8.39%.
evidence.shows: Each of the three terms in one picture.

transition_in.carries_over: The table of definitions.
transition_in.introduces: The three terms in it that a newcomer has not met.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The models are not exclusive: Kestrel & Pine runs four at once, and most merchants that have outgrown a single channel run at least two.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's four lines.
evidence.shows: Running several models at once is the normal case, which is why sharing becomes the question.

transition_in.carries_over: Nine models defined one by one.
transition_in.introduces: That a merchant runs several of them together.

sections.controlling_idea: A business model is a decision about who makes and keeps each promise of an order, and those answers decide what the systems must do.

advances_thesis.how: States the chapter's definition of a business model and shows, promise by promise, how the answers differ per model.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A business model is a decision about who makes and keeps each of the promises an order carries, and the answers, shown for the four models Kestrel & Pine runs and for the marketplace operator, decide what its systems must do.

sections.heading: In Practice: What the Public Record Says
sections.controlling_idea: Annual reports and official statistics confirm that the models differ in ways an architecture has to serve, and that one of them, marketplace operating, is a different business.

advances_thesis.how: Checks the definitions and the promise table against what companies and agencies publish, before the chapter turns to money.

flow.rationale: One finding per model in the order the chapter defined them: stores, the direct channel, marketplace operating, and business ordering last.

transition_in.carries_over: The models by definition and by who makes which promise.
transition_in.introduces: What annual reports and official statistics say about the same models, while the definitions are fresh.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The models and the promise table so far come from definitions and one fictional company; annual reports and official statistics show the same differences at full scale, in four findings.
For a retailer with stores, the stores are still the larger channel, and the architecture must treat them as one.

evidence.what: Online sales were 13.5% of German retail (2025) and 17.1% of US retail in the second quarter of 2026; Target's stores fulfilled 97.6% of its merchandise sales, including digital orders.
evidence.shows: Most sales still pass through stores, and a large retailer fulfils digital orders from them.
evidence.source: HDE Online-Monitor (2026); US Census Bureau (August 2026); Target annual report (March 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: The announcement of five findings from the public record.
transition_in.introduces: The first: stores as the larger channel.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A brand's mix of direct and wholesale sales moves from year to year, so the platform must serve both without a replatform each time.

evidence.what: NIKE Direct revenue of $17.7 billion against $18.8 billion a year earlier, 'primarily driven by a decrease in traffic'; VF's direct-to-consumer share is 44%.
evidence.shows: The direct share is not a one-way trend.
evidence.source: Nike annual report (July 2026); VF annual report (May 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: Stores as a channel in the record.
transition_in.introduces: The direct channel in the record, and that its share can fall.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Marketplace operating is a different business, built around sellers, listings, fees and payouts, which is why this book leaves it to other chapters and another book.

evidence.what: Amazon earned $172.2 billion from seller services in 2025 and is not the seller of record for third-party sales; Zalando's partner business was 32.1% of its GMV.
evidence.shows: An operator's revenue and liability sit with other sellers' orders.
evidence.source: Amazon and Zalando annual reports (2026); Marketplace Pulse (February 2026, analyst estimate)

transition_in.carries_over: Models a brand runs itself.
transition_in.introduces: The one model a brand should not take as its pattern.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Business ordering runs on two routes, the web shop and structured messages sent from the buyer's system, and the message route is the larger, so a wholesale architecture has to consider both.

evidence.what: Forrester's 2022 forecast expected US B2B e-commerce to reach about $3 trillion by 2027 and tracked EDI separately at about a fifth of transactions; the Eurostat comparison is in the models table.
evidence.shows: The message route is large enough to be counted on its own.

transition_in.carries_over: The consumer-facing models in the record.
transition_in.introduces: The business-to-business route in the record.

sections.heading: The Unit Economics of an Order
sections.controlling_idea: Each number in the unit economics of an order pulls on a different part of the platform.

advances_thesis.how: Ties each metric to the part of the architecture where it is won or lost.

transition_in.carries_over: Who makes which promise, as defined and as the public record confirms.
transition_in.introduces: What keeping those promises earns and costs per order, and where each number presses on the systems.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: How much money one order makes decides which promises a merchant can afford, and each number in that calculation pulls on a different part of the architecture.

evidence.what: Eight metrics (conversion rate, cart abandonment, average order value, gross margin, return rate, shipping cost and threshold, payment fees, customer acquisition cost), each with a plain definition, a dated public benchmark, Kestrel & Pine's 2026 figure and the part of the platform it pulls on.
evidence.shows: Every number has a place in the architecture where it is won or lost.
evidence.source: Littledata, Baymard, NRF, Coresight, annual reports, Regulation (EU) 2015/751, vendor price pages; Kestrel & Pine scenario ledger

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two of the numbers that look like design and finance matters are architecture matters: the reasons shoppers abandon carts are failures of a system to make a promise early and keep it, and payment fees depend on which provider the platform lets the merchant use.

evidence.what: At €27 million of online revenue the gap between 1.9% and 1.4% plus a fixed fee is six figures a year.
evidence.shows: A fee difference that sounds small is a platform decision worth making deliberately.
evidence.source: List prices in the table; Kestrel & Pine scenario ledger

transition_in.carries_over: The table of metrics.
transition_in.introduces: The two rows a newcomer is most likely to file under another department.

sections.heading: The Same Jacket in Three Lines: A Worked Example
sections.controlling_idea: One jacket sold through three lines is three businesses with three sets of promises.

advances_thesis.how: Works the promises and the numbers through one product, so the reader sees both differ by line.

transition_in.carries_over: The metrics one by one.
transition_in.introduces: One jacket's numbers in three lines.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: One Ridgewalker jacket, worked through the online, wholesale and marketplace lines, earns a different contribution (what is left of the price after the costs that come with each unit sold) in each and asks different things of the platform; the store line, which carries no parcel and no return parcel per order, is left out.

evidence.what: One unit through three lines: price, net revenue, landed cost €58, gross profit, fees, shipping, returns, marketing, an illustrative contribution of about €79, €36 and €62, and what each line needs from the platform; assumptions are marked.
evidence.shows: The same product is three different businesses once the costs of each line's promises are counted.
evidence.source: Kestrel & Pine scenario ledger; assumptions labelled in the table

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Read across, the table explains why the people Noor asked wanted different things: one jacket is three businesses with three sets of promises, and the architecture has to serve all three without pretending they are the same.

evidence.what: Figure 4: one jacket travelling to a consumer, a retailer and a marketplace, earning about €79, €36 and €62.
evidence.shows: The three contributions side by side, each with its own promises.

transition_in.introduces: What it explains about the requests in the opening scene.

sections.heading: Seasonality and the Peak
sections.controlling_idea: The peak is the last of the numbers: the load the whole chain of systems must be designed for, and the date that sets the calendar for change.

advances_thesis.how: Adds the one number the metrics table does not hold, the one that pulls on capacity; the conclusion and the questions use it.

transition_in.carries_over: The numbers of one order, per line.
transition_in.introduces: The number no single order shows: how orders bunch in time, which pulls on capacity.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every consumer model has a peak, and the peak is the load the systems must be designed for.

evidence.what: US e-commerce was 18.3% of retail sales in the fourth quarter of 2025 against 15.8% in the third; $44.2 billion of US online spending in Cyber Week 2025 with $16 million a minute at the peak; Shopify $14.6 billion over the Black Friday weekend with $5.1 million a minute.
evidence.shows: The peak is visible in national statistics and in vendors' own figures, per minute.
evidence.source: US Census Bureau (August 2026); Adobe Analytics (December 2025); Shopify (December 2025)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's own peak was smaller and no gentler: at 38 orders a minute the shop platform held, and the stock sync chain and the warehouse queue behind it did not.

evidence.what: Black Friday week 2026: 31,000 online orders, 10.6% of the year's; a peak hour of 2,300 orders, 38 a minute, at about 41 times an average hour's traffic; the Black Friday Oversell followed.
evidence.shows: The part that failed at peak was the chain behind the storefront.

transition_in.carries_over: The peak in public figures.
transition_in.introduces: The running example's peak and which part of the chain failed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two architectural facts come out of the peak: capacity is a property of the whole chain, every integration included, and the peak sets the calendar for change.

evidence.what: Hobbycraft postponed a website relaunch because 'we felt it was too risky to launch the website in peak trading'.
evidence.shows: Merchants plan changes around the peak.

evidence.what: Bergzicht's spring reorder in April.
evidence.shows: Wholesale has its own seasons, set by retailers' buying calendars.

transition_in.carries_over: What failed at Kestrel & Pine's peak.
transition_in.introduces: The two facts an architect takes from it.

flow.rationale: The claim with public figures, Kestrel & Pine's own peak, then the two architectural facts the case shows.

sections.heading: The Four Scale Stages
sections.controlling_idea: A scale stage is a shape of business, not a revenue band, and each transition adds joins between systems until the joins are the problem.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the four stages by shape and shows what each makes necessary.

flow.rationale: The definition, the running example's path, outside confirmation from vendors' price lists, then the second question the stages raise, when the hub systems arrive (what public sources say and the author's judgement), and last the slowed market, because it says what merchants at these stages now compete on, which is where the next section's incidents sit.

transition_in.carries_over: One merchant's models and numbers at one moment.
transition_in.introduces: How the shape of the business changes as it grows, in four stages.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A scale stage is a shape of business, described by how many channels create orders, how many locations hold stock, how many countries and brands are served and who runs the technology; revenue bands are only rough markers.

evidence.what: Four stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group) with typical size, shape, models run, what becomes necessary and the warning signs of outgrowing each.
evidence.shows: Each stage is recognisable by its shape and by what it makes necessary.
evidence.source: Kestrel & Pine scenario ledger; author's synthesis

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine passed through the first three stages, and its 2027 problems live in the Omnichannel stage, where three or four models share one stock and one catalog and the joins between a dozen systems become the business.

evidence.what: Starting in 2016–2018, Growing from 2019, Omnichannel from 2023.
evidence.shows: The company's path follows the shapes, not a revenue line.

evidence.what: Figure 5: each stage transition adds a channel or a location and a join between systems.
evidence.shows: The hubs arrive at the Omnichannel stage because the joins outnumber the boxes there.

transition_in.carries_over: The four stages.
transition_in.introduces: Where the running example stands and why its problems belong to that stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Vendors confirm the stages in their price lists: a merchant moves from a self-service plan to a negotiated contract at about the Growing-to-Omnichannel transition, the fee cliffs and feature gates in the tiers map the decisions the vendor expects at each size, and because the vendor counts GMV where the merchant counts orders, its roadmap is written for that metric.

evidence.what: Shopify from Basic at €28 a month to Plus 'from €2,100', with the third-party gateway fee falling from 2% to 0.2%; Shopware free until €1 million of GMV a year, then 'from €600' a month, priced on GMV; most Shopify merchants on its two smallest plans while most GMV comes from Plus and enterprise.
evidence.shows: Vendors price by the same steps the chapter calls stages.
evidence.source: Shopify and Shopware pricing pages (n.d., accessed November 2026); Shopify annual report 2025

transition_in.carries_over: The stages as defined and as Kestrel & Pine lived them.
transition_in.introduces: Outside confirmation from vendors' price lists.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Public sources give no revenue threshold for buying an order, product or warehouse management system; they point to the work instead: scattered content, slow channel launches, several sales channels and stock locations.

evidence.what: Akeneo's signs that a PIM is needed; practitioner guides for order management systems.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's lines share facts (a price, an order, a stock figure, a refund) that more than one system holds and nobody owns, each line has failed there in its own way, and every failure was found and repaired the same way.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the cost of leaving the shared facts unowned, in four incidents.

flow.rationale: Four incidents in the same shape (a fact held in two places, a difference somebody noticed), then what they share: the common remedy is only visible after all four.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine has been losing money on margin, returns and operations: its lines share facts that more than one system holds and nobody owns, and each line has failed there in its own way.
The Price Drift: two lines sold one jacket at two prices for nine days because a price-list sync failed silently, and a marketplace noticed before the merchant did.

evidence.what: October 2026: €179 on the German storefront against €199 elsewhere for nine days; 410 orders, about €8,200 of margin and a price-parity warning.
evidence.shows: A price with more than one owner drifts, and a marketplace's parity rule turns the drift into a penalty.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Wholesale on a consumer platform: over a third of wholesale orders are born in a system the consumer line never sees, and when the retailer compared the pallet labels with the despatch advice and found they did not match, it deducted the difference: a promise no consumer system knows how to make.

evidence.what: 62% of wholesale orders through the platform's B2B features and 38% keyed into the ERP; the ASN Chargeback of Q3 2026, €14,200 deducted by Bergzicht.
evidence.shows: A wholesale promise fails on systems built for consumer orders.

sections.heading: The Choices: One Stack, Many Stacks or a Shared Core
sections.controlling_idea: A merchant with several models can run one stack, a stack per line or a shared core with line-specific edges, and should own the shared facts once from the moment the joins start to cost money.

advances_thesis.how: Answers the chapter's practical question: what the lines share is owned once, what differs stays at the edges.

flow.rationale: The three arrangements in the order a merchant meets them, then the author's choice: the recommendation needs all three described first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A stack is the set of systems a business line runs on, and a merchant running several business models has three realistic ways to arrange its stacks, each right somewhere.
One stack for every line is the simplest to run and the cheapest to integrate, and it fits until one line's promises do not fit the platform's model.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The models, the numbers and the stages answer one question from three sides: what the lines of a business can share. They can share facts (the product, the price list, the stock, the order record) and cannot share promises, and a stage is the count of promises a merchant makes at once; so the same table that tells the models apart also says which facts need one owner and when.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant that has filled in who makes which promise for each line, and measured its numbers, can say where its architecture must be strong and can refuse an architecture copied from a company with a different model or shape.

callback.to: The jacket sold by the web shop to a shopper and by the wholesale team to a retail chain, where software built for the first sale failed the conditions of the second.
callback.how: The reader can now say what that software lacked: the two sales can share the product, the price list, the stock and the order record, and each needs its own promises kept at its own edge.

takeaway.content: Fill in the who-makes-which-promise table for each line, measure the numbers nobody has measured, and take the eight questions to the business.
